title: Social Network Analysis
note: 0–2 min. Welcome. This deck is designed for a 180-minute meeting including a 15-minute break. The advice networks are synthetic teaching examples.

title: Today’s learning goals
note: 2–5 min. Explain that interpretation matters as much as calculation. Ask which outcome is least familiar.

title: Introductions
note: 5–15 min. Keep introductions brief. With a large class, use pairs and collect a few examples.

title: The course ahead
note: 15–18 min. Explain the progression. Do not present the 2025 assessment as confirmed 2026 policy. Confirm current assessment and deadlines separately before class.

title: Our three-hour session
note: 18–20 min. Orient students to the break and practical work.

title: Who can reach a new opportunity?
note: 20–23 min. Ask students to predict what individual-level data could miss. This is a hypothetical example, not an empirical causal claim.

title: Same actors, different relationships
note: 23–28 min. Compare two graphs with six nodes and five edges each. Left has an isolate and a bridge; right is a connected path. Ask who could receive a message if it travels only along observed ties. Equal size and density do not imply equal reachability.

title: The relational perspective
note: 28–32 min. A conventional table can store relational data too. The distinction is the substantive unit and dependence structure, not the file format. Mention that ties sharing actors may be dependent; independent-observation assumptions need care.

title: A network is a set of actors and ties
note: 32–35 min. Use nodes/vertices and edges/ties as synonyms, then stick with nodes and ties. E is a set; m = |E| is its size.

title: Our running example: an advice network
note: 35–40 min. Synthetic six-person research group. Initially treat a tie as a confirmed advice relationship without direction. A–B, A–C, B–C, C–D, D–E; F has no observed ties. Later introduce a distinct directed nomination version.

title: Weak ties and access to new information
note: 40–45 min. Use C–D as a structural bridge in our undirected example. Tie strength has not yet been measured, so do not call it weak based on its position alone. Source: Granovetter (1973), The Strength of Weak Ties, https://doi.org/10.1086/225469. Avoid a universal claim that weak ties spread all information better.

title: The research question defines the network
note: 45–49 min. This introduces the directed nomination version, not a claim that earlier undirected data encoded direction. Make clear that arrow direction must be stated.

title: Directed, undirected, and weighted ties
note: 49–53 min. Friendship survey nominations may be directed, even if everyday friendship is described as mutual. Weighted ties can represent frequency, intensity, duration, or distance; meanings differ.

title: Arrow direction changes the interpretation
note: 53–57 min. Directed version has A→B, A→C, B→C, C→D, D→E. Arrow means seeker→source. C is named by two people and names one source. Do not infer frequency from binary degree.

title: A network boundary is a research decision
note: 57–61 min. Removing F raises undirected density from 5/15 to 5/10 without changing any observed edge. Explain this now, calculate it later. Distinguish whole-network and ego-network designs briefly.

title: No observed tie can mean several things
note: 61–65 min. Missing is not automatically zero. Discuss one example of a missing central respondent. Explain that network data can expose relationships involving people who did not provide data themselves.

title: Activity: define a network study
note: 65–75 min. Pairs: 2 min choose question, 5 min specify design, 3 min prepare explanation. Use hypothetical examples rather than collecting classmates’ sensitive nominations.

title: Discussion: would your data answer the question?
note: 75–80 min. Invite two pairs. Challenge causal claims gently: a pattern of contact does not establish influence. Ask how they would protect identities and relational information.

title: Break
note: 80–95 min. Resume with the six-node example.

title: One network, several representations
note: 95–98 min. These are related representations, but a layout alone is not a complete data model and an edge list alone omits isolates.

title: Edge list and node list
note: 98–102 min. Undirected version: store each pair once. A node table may contain attributes; retain all six actors, including F.

title: Adjacency matrix: the same undirected network
note: 102–107 min. Rows and columns use the same node order. A_ij=1 if there is a tie. Undirected matrix is symmetric. Diagonal zeros assume no self-loops. Every undirected edge appears twice.

title: Activity: change the representation
note: 107–115 min. 6 min work, 2 min compare. Directed answer is on the next slide. Check students preserve the all-zero row and column for F.

title: Answer: the directed advice matrix
note: 115–120 min. Convention: row=sender (seeker), column=receiver (advice source). A→B occupies row A, column B. Row sums are out-degree; column sums are in-degree.

title: Degree counts incident ties
note: 120–124 min. All examples here are simple binary graphs without loops. Strength sums weights and is a different measure. An isolate has degree zero; low positive degree does not mean isolation.

title: Density is the fraction of possible ties
note: 124–128 min. These formulas assume at most one edge per eligible pair, no self-loops, and n≥2. They are not formulas for summing interaction weights. Density is undefined by these formulas for n<2.

title: Activity: describe the six-person group
note: 128–135 min. Let students calculate before showing answers. Ask one pair to explain the denominator and another to interpret C’s directed degree.

title: Answer: degree, density, and the missing isolate
note: 135–138 min. Undirected degrees sum to 10 = 2m. Directed in-degree and out-degree each sum to m=5. Omitting F raises density without adding a relationship.

title: What these measures can and cannot tell us
note: 138–140 min. Return to the two networks at the start. Optional extension: mean degree = 2m/n = density × (n−1) for simple undirected networks. This is a relation between averages, not a claim about the full degree distribution.

title: R practical: build and inspect the network
note: 140–143 min. Allow a fallback: students without working R pair with someone who has it. Notebook needs igraph only. Install packages before class where possible.

title: A minimal network in R
note: 143–147 min. Explain why vertices=nodes is essential. Do not spend time on advanced visualization packages.

title: Practical task 1: check your answers
note: 147–153 min. Six minutes. Expected: n=6, m=5, degree=(2,2,3,2,1,0), density=1/3. See notebook for commands and checks.

title: Practical task 2: change one relationship
note: 153–160 min. Seven minutes. Answer: m=6, density=6/15=.4; E changes 1→2, F changes 0→1. Network becomes connected. Density alone does not express this qualitative change.

title: Practical task 3: direction and interpretation
note: 160–166 min. Six minutes. C has highest in-degree=2; A highest out-degree=2. Reversing arrows preserves density and swaps in/out degree. Original graph has no E–F addition in this task.

title: One graph can have several layouts
note: 166–170 min. Four minutes. Layout changes do not change adjacency, degree, or density. The fixed arrangement was chosen for teaching and does not encode geography.

title: Classic results need careful interpretation
note: 170–173 min. Optional brief context rather than a new theory unit. Travers & Milgram (1969): 64 completed chains from 296 starters; mean 5.2 intermediaries in completed chains. This does not establish universal six-step reachability. https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-readings/travers69smallworld.pdf. Broido & Clauset (2019), Scale-free networks are rare: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08746-5. Preferential attachment is one generative model, not established by a hub-shaped plot.

title: Exit question
note: 173–177 min. Individual written response. Expected: an isolate may be missing; omitting it changes the denominator from 15 to 10 and raises density from .333 to .5. Five actors is consistent with the running example, but in a real dataset investigate rather than assume.

title: What you should now be able to do
note: 177–180 min. Ask students to name one remaining uncertainty. Next class: paths, components, and graph structure.

title: Reading and sources
note: Reference slide, outside timed teaching. Granovetter https://doi.org/10.1086/225469; Travers & Milgram https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-readings/travers69smallworld.pdf; Broido & Clauset https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08746-5; Borgatti et al. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1165821. Reworked from ADAIII_2025/meeting_slides/ADA_III_Meeting_01.pdf and the 2025 first-session notebook. All network data and diagrams in this deck are synthetic instructional examples.
